summary:
Ondo State stands under Nigeria's national framework. Same-sex conduct has been illegal across the country since 1916, and the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014, passed by the House of Representatives on 30 May 2013 and signed by President Goodluck Jonathan in January 2014, criminalises all forms of same-sex union with up to 14 years' imprisonment. The Act's reach extends beyond the couple: the UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office travel advisory reported on 19 August 2026 warns that participants and guests at same-sex weddings are also liable. Human Rights Watch records that the statute additionally bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, with penalties of 10 to 14 years, and that police have invoked it to justify torture and arbitrary arrest.

The Shari'a penalty layer, under which male sodomy can be punished by death, operates only in the twelve states with Shari'a-based criminal codes and does not extend to Ondo. As a southern state, Ondo sits under the secular Criminal Code, where Section 217 makes it a felony for any male to commit or procure an act of gross indecency with another male, in public or in private, punishable by three years' imprisonment. The maximum penalty recorded for the southern portion of the country is a life sentence. An overview of LGBT rights in Nigeria reports no state-specific divergence for Ondo and no protective statute of its own.

The interpretive breadth of the southern offence is unsettled. Victor Oluwasina Ayeni, senior lecturer in law at Adekunle Ajasin University in Ondo State, observed in a January 2017 book chapter that Section 217 fails to define what constitutes an act of gross indecency, leaving the scope of the felony to be fixed case by case.

Nigeria offers no legal recognition of gender identity, no anti-discrimination protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and no recognition of same-sex relationships. Trans identity is not named in the national statute, but gender expression is exposed: Reuters reported in September 2022 that transgender Nigerians live under fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public, and whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here.

Entry screening and travel advice treat the country as high risk for LGBT visitors. The UK Home Office country policy and information note of June 2025 documents the national criminal framework applying across all states and records countrywide patterns of arrest, detention and mob violence against LGBT people. The FCDO advisory of 19 August 2026 warns LGBT travellers of arrest, violence, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and of death-penalty risk under Shari'a in northern states.

Trans-specific violence is documented. On 9 August 2024 the beaten body of the 33-year-old Nigerian transgender TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama was found on the Katampe-Mabushi expressway in Abuja; police opened a 'thorough and discreet' investigation. Six months later no suspects had been charged. Enforcement of the climate that produced the killing is not limited to formal charges: in March 2025 Lagos police struck a 24-year-old man in the mouth with a gun butt and released him only after he paid part of a 50,000 naira bribe demanded for looking gay, and the Thomson Reuters Foundation documented kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

The only trans-specific imprisonment case in these sources concerns Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye). She pleaded guilty to four counts of naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine, served in a maximum-security prison in Lagos and ending with her release on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing openly asked which prison the authorities would keep the crossdresser in, indicating that placement between male and female sections was left to official discretion. An October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that housing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.
tangentialFactors:
The pattern documented nationally is one of mob violence and mass arrest alongside formal prosecution, and the UK Home Office note records these harms as countrywide rather than confined to any one state. The Home Office also confirms that the twelve northern states' Shari'a penal codes, with penalties up to death by stoning, remain in force, which is the layer of Nigerian law that does not apply to Ondo.

Community-level predation runs alongside state enforcement. Kito gangs use dating applications to arrange meetings at which victims are assaulted and blackmailed with threats of outing, a risk independent of whether any charge is ever brought.

Official hostility shows in police conduct as well as statute: the March 2025 Lagos case indicates that looking gay can be treated as grounds for a beating and an extortion demand regardless of evidence.
localsOnly:
Residents of Ondo State live under the secular Criminal Code rather than a Shari'a penal code, and the gross-indecency offence of Section 217 is the operative provision for male same-sex conduct in public or private. No state-specific protective statute or documented enforcement divergence applies in Ondo.

Legal scholarship within the state has flagged the ambiguity of that provision. Victor Oluwasina Ayeni of Adekunle Ajasin University in Ondo State wrote in a January 2017 chapter that the Code never defines what an act of gross indecency is, which leaves residents exposed to a charge whose elements are fixed after the fact.

Prison placement for transgender detainees is left to discretion rather than rule. The October 2024 panel found that housing Bobrisky in a maximum-security facility breached the Nigerian Correctional Service Act, but the Act's application to gender-diverse prisoners was not settled by that finding, and press coverage at the time openly speculated about which section she would be held in.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory names Ondo in connection with a specific arrest, prosecution or conviction of a trans person. The state's position is derived from its status as a southern state under the national framework, not from Ondo-specific enforcement data, and Ondo does not appear in the encyclopaedic overview of LGBT rights in Nigeria at all.

The scope of Section 217's 'gross indecency' is unresolved on these sources: the only treatment of the term is the observation that it is undefined, and no case law applying it in Ondo is recorded here.

Whether the cross-dressing proposals reported by Reuters in September 2022 have since been enacted is not settled by the material available for this record.

Whether the FCDO travel advisory affects entry decisions, visa screening or detention practice for trans visitors at Nigerian points of entry is not stated in any of these sources; the advisory is a warning, not an entry rule.

No data is available here on how Ondo State correctional facilities would house a trans detainee, or on any state-level police directive concerning gender expression.
